The distinction between reducible and irreducible representations is central to Wiles’s modularity-lifting argument. For an elliptic curve \(E\) over \(\mathbb{Q}\), the \(p\)-adic Tate module gives a continuous Galois representation \(\rho(E,p^\infty)\), and reducing it modulo \(p\) yields the residual representation \(\bar{\rho}(E,p): G_{\mathbb{Q}} \to \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)\). This residual representation is called irreducible if it has no proper invariant one-dimensional subspace, and reducible if, after a suitable change of basis, it is upper triangular and therefore built from two characters. The modular lifting problem asks whether the modularity of \(\bar{\rho}(E,p)\) can be lifted to modularity of the full \(p\)-adic representation, and hence of \(E\) itself. Reducibility matters because it changes the deformation theory of the representation: the space of possible lifts, the automorphisms of the residual object, and the local conditions at primes dividing the conductor behave very differently in the two cases.

When \(\bar{\rho}(E,p)\) is irreducible, the deformation problem is comparatively rigid. Schur’s lemma implies that the only endomorphisms commuting with the representation are scalars, so the functor of deformations is representable by a universal deformation ring \(R\). Wiles, with Taylor’s patching method, compares \(R\) with a Hecke algebra \(T\) acting on modular forms of the appropriate level and weight. The map \(R \to T\) is shown to be an isomorphism by controlling tangent spaces, obstructions, and auxiliary primes. Once this isomorphism is established, the modular point of \(T\) corresponding to \(\bar{\rho}(E,p)\) lifts to a \(p\)-adic modular form whose associated Galois representation is \(\rho(E,p^\infty)\). Thus, in the irreducible case, modularity of one residual representation forces modularity of the elliptic curve.

The reducible case requires a different argument because the residual representation decomposes into characters and may admit nontrivial extensions. The deformation space is then less rigid: lifts can split, become non-minimal, or acquire extra automorphisms, so the simple comparison between a universal deformation ring and a Hecke algebra may fail or need modification. Wiles therefore treats reducible residual representations by additional techniques, such as level raising and level lowering, congruences between modular forms, or by choosing another prime for which the residual representation is irreducible when possible. For semistable elliptic curves relevant to Fermat’s Last Theorem, this case-by-case analysis is essential: it ensures that no Frey curve can escape the modularity theorem merely because its mod-\(p\) representation is reducible. In short, reducibility is not a minor technicality; it determines the structure of the lifting problem and therefore the proof strategy.

The passage from a modular residual representation to a modular \(p\)-adic representation is the heart of Wiles’s argument. For a semistable elliptic curve \(E\), the representation \(\rho(E,p)\) is the action of the absolute Galois group of \(\mathbb{Q}\) on the \(p\)-torsion points \(E[p]\), while \(\rho(E,p^{\infty})\) is the compatible system of actions on the \(p\)-power torsion, equivalently on the \(p\)-adic Tate module. Wiles’s lifting theorem says that if the finite residual representation \(\rho(E,p)\) occurs in a modular form, then the entire \(p\)-adic representation is modular. Deformation theory formalizes this by studying all lifts of \(\rho(E,p)\) to complete local rings subject to local conditions such as semistability, fixed determinant, and prescribed ramification. The goal is to identify the universal deformation ring with a Hecke algebra acting on modular forms, thereby showing that the given elliptic curve’s representation is one of the modular lifts.

When \(\rho(E,p)\) is irreducible, the deformation problem is comparatively rigid. Irreducibility means that the representation has no proper invariant subspace over \(\mathbb{F}_p\), so its centralizer consists only of scalar matrices. This small automorphism group makes the deformation functor well behaved: local deformation rings are easier to describe, global obstructions are controlled by Galois cohomology, and the universal deformation ring has a predictable dimension. In this setting, Wiles and Taylor can use patching arguments to compare the deformation ring with the corresponding Hecke algebra. Because there are no nontrivial invariant lines, a modular lift is less likely to be distorted by accidental extensions, and the modularity of a single residual representation can be propagated to the full \(p\)-adic representation. Thus the irreducible case provides the main technical engine of the proof.

The reducible case is more delicate because \(\rho(E,p)\) preserves a line and therefore appears as an extension of two characters. Such representations can have nontrivial self-extensions, larger automorphism groups, and more complicated local deformation spaces; the universal deformation ring may fail to be smooth, and the Hecke algebra may contain Eisenstein components that do not correspond to genuine modular elliptic curves. Consequently, the same lifting argument cannot be applied without additional input. Wiles’s proof handles this by separating the cases and using auxiliary arguments, including the possibility of choosing a different prime for which the residual representation is irreducible, level-lowering techniques, and careful analysis of Selmer groups and congruences between modular forms. This branching is not a minor technicality: it reflects the fact that reducible representations encode extension data that can obstruct a direct identification of deformation rings with Hecke algebras, so the proof must establish modularity by a different route.

The divergence between genital and brain sexual differentiation is best understood as a consequence of heterochrony and regional molecular specificity. In mammals, the Y-linked SRY gene initiates testis development, after which fetal Leydig cells secrete testosterone and Sertoli cells secrete anti-Müllerian hormone; external genitalia are masculinized primarily by dihydrotestosterone during a relatively early first-trimester window. By contrast, sexually dimorphic hypothalamic and limbic nuclei such as the central subdivision of the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BSTc) and the third interstitial nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus (INAH3) may be patterned later, during mid-to-late gestation and even postnatally, through testosterone, estradiol produced by local aromatization, androgen and estrogen receptor expression, 5α-reductase activity, and neurosteroid synthesis within glia and neurons. Because these nuclei differ from peripheral tissues in blood–brain barrier permeability, receptor density, steroidogenic enzyme expression, epigenetic state, and timing of neurogenesis, apoptosis, microglial pruning, and synaptic maturation, they can follow a developmental trajectory that is not identical to that of the genitals or the body as a whole. Sex-chromosome complement and escape genes, imprinting, and gonad-independent genetic programs may further bias regional brain development, producing a mosaic rather than a uniformly masculinized or feminized organism.

Prenatal environmental factors can modulate these pathways by altering the hormonal milieu or the sensitivity of developing neural circuits. Maternal stress, placental insufficiency, hypoxia, inflammation, immune activation, and cytokine exposure can change fetal hypothalamic–pituitary–adrenal and gonadal axis activity, while placental enzymes such as aromatase and 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 normally protect the fetus from excess maternal androgens or glucocorticoids. Endocrine-disrupting chemicals—phthalates, bisphenol A, organochlorine pesticides, and some pharmaceuticals—can antagonize androgen receptors, alter steroidogenesis, or mimic estrogens, thereby shifting the balance of signals that pattern sexually dimorphic nuclei. Nutritional and metabolic conditions, including folate, choline, iodine, thyroid hormone, insulin, and glucose availability, also influence neurodevelopment and epigenetic regulation. Human conditions such as congenital adrenal hyperplasia, androgen insensitivity, 5α-reductase deficiency, and maternal androgen-secreting tumors provide natural experiments showing that prenatal androgen exposure can influence gender-typical behavior and some neural phenotypes, but they do not establish a one-to-one mapping between hormone exposure and gender identity.

Does this demonstrate that gender identity is hardwired prior to birth? Not conclusively. Postmortem studies reporting that BSTc or INAH3 dimensions in some transgender women resemble those of cisgender women are intriguing but limited by small samples, selection bias, tissue-processing variability, age, cause of death, HIV status, and, crucially, prior hormone therapy, which can alter brain structure. Other studies have found inconsistent results, with some nuclei tracking natal sex rather than gender identity, and no single hypothalamic or limbic nucleus has been validated as a biomarker of identity. Even if prenatal biological factors bias the development of circuits involved in self-representation, interoception, social cognition, and sexual behavior, gender identity is likely an emergent property of distributed networks shaped by ongoing neuroplasticity, embodiment, language, social experience, and psychological development. The most defensible conclusion is that prenatal neuroendocrine and genetic mechanisms may contribute probabilistically to gender identity, but they do not prove that identity is fixed, binary, or fully determined before birth.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Nearest-neighbor retrieval for French literary lines using character n-gram
TF-IDF vectorization and cosine similarity.

The script is dependency-free and uses only the Python standard library.
"""

import math
import re
from collections import Counter
from typing import Dict, List, Tuple


CORPUS: List[str] = [
    "D'où me vient ce désordre, Aufide, et que veut dire",
    "Madame, il était temps qu'il vous vînt du secours:",
    "Ah! Monsieur, c'est donc vous?",
    "Ami, j'ai beau rêver, toute ma rêverie",
    "Ne me parle plus tant de joie et d'hyménéé;",
    "Il est vrai, Cléobule, et je veux l'avouer",
    "Laisse-moi mon chagrin, tout injuste qu'il est;",
    "Ton frère, je l'avoue, a beacoup de mérite",
    "J'en demeure d'accord, chacun a sa méthode;",
    "Pour prix de votre amour que vous peignez extrême,",
]


def normalize(text: str) -> str:
    """
    Lowercase the text, replace punctuation with spaces, and collapse whitespace.
    Accented French characters are preserved.
    """
    text = text.lower()
    text = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", text, flags=re.UNICODE)
    text = text.replace("_", " ")
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text).strip()
    return text


def character_ngrams(text: str, n_min: int = 2, n_max: int = 4) -> List[str]:
    """
    Generate all character n-grams of length n_min through n_max.
    """
    grams: List[str] = []
    for n in range(n_min, n_max + 1):
        for i in range(len(text) - n + 1):
            grams.append(text[i:i + n])
    return grams


def build_tfidf_vectors(
    documents: List[str],
    n_min: int = 2,
    n_max: int = 4,
) -> List[Dict[str, float]]:
    """
    Convert each document into a sparse TF-IDF vector over character n-grams.

    Each vector is L2-normalized so that cosine similarity can be computed
    as a simple dot product.
    """
    normalized = [normalize(doc) for doc in documents]
    counts = [Counter(character_ngrams(doc, n_min, n_max)) for doc in normalized]

    document_frequency: Counter = Counter()
    for count in counts:
        for gram in count:
            document_frequency[gram] += 1

    n_docs = len(documents)
    vectors: List[Dict[str, float]] = []

    for count in counts:
        total_grams = sum(count.values())
        vector: Dict[str, float] = {}

        if total_grams == 0:
            vectors.append(vector)
            continue

        for gram, freq in count.items():
            tf = freq / total_grams
            idf = math.log((1 + n_docs) / (1 + document_frequency[gram])) + 1.0
            vector[gram] = tf * idf

        norm = math.sqrt(sum(value * value for value in vector.values()))
        if norm > 0:
            vector = {gram: value / norm for gram, value in vector.items()}

        vectors.append(vector)

    return vectors


def cosine_similarity_sparse(a: Dict[str, float], b: Dict[str, float]) -> float:
    """
    Compute cosine similarity between two sparse vectors represented as dicts.

    Because the vectors are already L2-normalized, cosine similarity is the
    dot product of the two vectors.
    """
    if len(a) > len(b):
        a, b = b, a

    return sum(value * b.get(gram, 0.0) for gram, value in a.items())


def pairwise_similarity_matrix(vectors: List[Dict[str, float]]) -> List[List[float]]:
    """
    Build the full pairwise cosine similarity matrix.
    """
    n = len(vectors)
    matrix = [[0.0] * n for _ in range(n)]

    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i, n):
            sim = cosine_similarity_sparse(vectors[i], vectors[j])
            matrix[i][j] = sim
            matrix[j][i] = sim

    return matrix


def nearest_neighbors(
    vectors: List[Dict[str, float]],
    exclude_self: bool = True,
) -> List[Tuple[int, int, float]]:
    """
    For each line i, return the index j of the closest line and the similarity.
    """
    n = len(vectors)
    results: List[Tuple[int, int, float]] = []

    for i in range(n):
        best_j = -1
        best_sim = -1.0

        for j in range(n):
            if exclude_self and i == j:
                continue

            sim = cosine_similarity_sparse(vectors[i], vectors[j])

            if sim > best_sim:
                best_sim = sim
                best_j = j

        results.append((i, best_j, best_sim))

    return results


def main() -> None:
    vectors = build_tfidf_vectors(CORPUS, n_min=2, n_max=4)
    similarity = pairwise_similarity_matrix(vectors)
    neighbors = nearest_neighbors(vectors)

    print("Pairwise cosine similarity matrix (rounded):")
    header = "     " + " ".join(f"{j:>6}" for j in range(len(CORPUS)))
    print(header)

    for i, row in enumerate(similarity):
        print(f"{i:>4} " + " ".join(f"{value:>6.3f}" for value in row))

    print("\nNearest neighbor for each line (self excluded):")
    for i, j, sim in neighbors:
        print(f"{i}: {CORPUS[i]!r}")
        print(f"   -> {j}: {CORPUS[j]!r} (cosine={sim:.4f})")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Although the equations are deterministic, the attractor is not a simple closed curve or torus; it is a bounded invariant set with a fractal geometry, often described as having two lobes or wings. The flow continuously stretches trajectories in some directions while contracting them in others, and the dissipative nature of the system causes phase-space volumes to shrink. To remain bounded, the flow must fold the stretched material back onto itself, producing a layered, self-similar structure. This stretching-and-folding mechanism is geometrically responsible for the attractor’s nonperiodic motion and for the fact that nearby trajectories can separate rapidly while still remaining confined to the same global set.

A trajectory of the Lorenz system is a curve in phase space, with coordinates \((x, y, z)\), generated by the vector field defined by the differential equations. Given an initial condition, the solution is unique and deterministic, so the future path is completely fixed by the present state. For the standard parameters, most initial conditions in a large basin of attraction approach the Lorenz attractor after a transient. Once on the attractor, the trajectory never repeats exactly, yet it remains bounded and visits the two lobes in an irregular sequence. The two trajectories in the script start only \(10^{-4}\) apart in \(x\), but the nonlinear feedback terms cause their separation to grow exponentially at first and then fluctuate as the trajectories are folded by the attractor. This illustrates sensitive dependence on initial conditions: the global geometry is stable, but the precise timing of lobe transitions is not.

The maximal Lyapunov exponent provides a quantitative measure of this sensitivity. For a deterministic flow \(\dot{x} = f(x)\), consider an infinitesimal perturbation \(\delta x(t)\) between two nearby trajectories. Its evolution is governed by the variational equation \(\dot{\delta x} = J(x(t))\delta x\), where \(J\) is the Jacobian matrix of \(f\) evaluated along the reference trajectory. The maximal Lyapunov exponent is defined as  
\[
\lambda_{\max} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{t} \ln \left( \frac{\|\delta x(t)\|}{\|\delta x(0)\|} \right),
\]
when the limit exists, or equivalently as the largest asymptotic exponential growth rate of perturbations. A positive \(\lambda_{\max}\) indicates that typical infinitesimal separations grow exponentially, which is a hallmark of chaos. In dissipative systems such as Lorenz, the sum of all Lyapunov exponents is negative because phase-space volume contracts, but the largest exponent is positive, producing chaotic dynamics on a strange attractor.

Academic explanation

Circular topological fingerprints such as ECFP4 encode molecular structure by iteratively expanding atom-centered neighborhoods. For each atom, an initial invariant is computed from element, degree, formal charge, hybridization, aromaticity, ring membership, and hydrogen count. At iteration k, the identifier of an atom is updated by hashing its previous identifier together with the sorted identifiers of its bonded neighbors, thereby capturing the topology of a radius-k circular substructure. ECFP4 corresponds to radius 2, so each hashed feature represents the atom-centered environment up to two bonds away. The resulting set of hashed identifiers is folded into a fixed-length bit vector, commonly 2048 bits, by modulo arithmetic; a bit is set if at least one substructure hashes to that position. This process converts a graph into a sparse binary feature vector whose bits approximate presence or absence of local chemical environments, while ignoring global coordinates and preserving topological connectivity. Because hashing is lossy, rare substructures may collide, but the fixed-length representation enables fast database searching.

Once molecules are represented as binary vectors, similarity is commonly measured with the Tanimoto coefficient, also called the Jaccard similarity. Let A and B be the sets of bit positions set to 1 in two fingerprints. The Tanimoto similarity is T(A,B)=|A∩B|/|A∪B|, equivalently c/(a+b-c), where a and b are the numbers of set bits in the two fingerprints and c is the number of shared set bits. The corresponding Tanimoto or Jaccard distance is D_J=1-T=1-|A∩B|/|A∪B|, ranging from 0 for identical bit patterns to 1 for completely disjoint fingerprints. In cheminformatics, this metric is appropriate for binary fingerprints because it normalizes by the union of features, penalizing both missing shared substructures and non-shared features. For count fingerprints, variants such as the Tanimoto distance on count vectors or Dice coefficients may be used, but the binary formulation remains the standard for ECFP4 similarity screening.

Interpretation of similarity thresholds is context-dependent rather than absolute. In virtual screening, Tanimoto values above roughly 0.85 are often treated as very high similarity and may indicate close analogs or scaffold retention, whereas values around 0.60–0.75 can suggest partial pharmacophoric or topological resemblance useful for hit expansion. Values below 0.40–0.50 usually imply low structural overlap, although biologically active compounds can be dissimilar in ECFP space because activity depends on 3D shape, electronic properties, and protein interactions; conversely, activity cliffs can make small topological changes produce large biological differences. Medicinal chemists therefore use thresholds as heuristic filters: high thresholds reduce false positives and preserve scaffold integrity, while lower thresholds increase chemical diversity and scaffold-hopping potential but raise the risk of inactive hits. Because ECFP4 is a topological approximation, similarity scores should be combined with docking, machine-learning predictions, synthetic accessibility, and experimental validation rather than used as a sole decision rule.

import time
import gc

N = 100_000
Q = 50_000
QUERY_COUNT = 25_000
UPDATE_COUNT = Q - QUERY_COUNT
SEED = 12345


def seg_build(arr):
    """Build an iterative segment tree from arr."""
    n = len(arr)
    size = 1
    while size < n:
        size <<= 1

    tree = [0] * (2 * size)
    tree[size:size + n] = arr

    for i in range(size - 1, 0, -1):
        tree[i] = tree[i << 1] + tree[(i << 1) | 1]

    return tree, size


def seg_update(tree, size, index, value):
    """Point update: set arr[index] = value."""
    i = index + size
    tree[i] = value
    i >>= 1

    while i:
        tree[i] = tree[i << 1] + tree[(i << 1) | 1]
        i >>= 1


def seg_query(tree, size, left, right):
    """Inclusive range sum query: sum(arr[left:right + 1])."""
    left += size
    right += size
    total = 0

    while left <= right:
        if left & 1:
            total += tree[left]
            left += 1

        if not (right & 1):
            total += tree[right]
            right -= 1

        left >>= 1
        right >>= 1

    return total

    """
    Generate intermixed point updates and range-sum queries.

    Operation encoding:
      (0, index, value)  -> point update
      (1, left, right)   -> inclusive range sum query
    """
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    ops = []

    update_count = q - query_count

    for _ in range(update_count):
        index = rng.randrange(n)
        value = rng.randint(-1000, 1000)
        ops.append((0, index, value))

    for _ in range(query_count):
        left = rng.randrange(n)

        # Mostly short ranges, with some medium ranges, to keep the naive
        # linear scan feasible while still exposing the asymptotic gap.
        if rng.random() < 0.75:
            length = rng.randint(1, 100)
        else:
            length = rng.randint(1000, 2000)

        right = min(n - 1, left + length - 1)
        ops.append((1, left, right))

    rng.shuffle(ops)
    return ops

    """Execute all operations using the segment tree."""
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    tree, size = seg_build(initial)
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    build_time = t1 - t0

    results = []
    update = seg_update
    query = seg_query

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for kind, x, y in ops:
        if kind == 0:
            update(tree, size, x, y)
        else:
            results.append(query(tree, size, x, y))
    t1 = time.perf_counter()

    return build_time, t1 - t0, results


def run_naive(initial, ops):

    arr = initial.copy()
    results = []

    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for kind, x, y in ops:
        if kind == 0:
            arr[x] = y

    ops = generate_operations(N, Q, QUERY_COUNT, SEED)

    scanned = sum(y - x + 1 for kind, x, y in ops if kind == 1)

    gc.disable()

        naive_time, naive_results = run_naive(initial, ops)
    finally:

    if seg_results != naive_results:
        raise SystemExit("Correctness check failed: segment tree and naive results differ.")

    seg_total = seg_build_time + seg_op_time

    print("Benchmark configuration")
    print(f"  N = {N:,}")
    print(f"  Q = {Q:,} ({UPDATE_COUNT:,} updates, {QUERY_COUNT:,} range-sum queries)")
    print(f"  Naive elements scanned by queries = {scanned:,}")
    print()
    print("Timings")
    print(f"  Segment tree build:       {seg_build_time:.6f} s")
    print(f"  Segment tree operations:  {seg_op_time:.6f} s")
    print(f"  Segment tree total:       {seg_total:.6f} s")
    print(f"  Naive array total:        {naive_time:.6f} s")
    print(f"  Speedup (naive / segment): {naive_time / seg_total:.2f}x")


if __name__ == "__main__":

"""
Synthesize a 1-second C-major triad with logarithmically decaying 2nd and 3rd
harmonics, then extract and identify FFT peaks using NumPy and SciPy.
"""

import numpy as np
from scipy.fft import rfft, rfftfreq
from scipy.signal import find_peaks, windows


def main() -> None:
    # Audio parameters
    fs = 44100
    duration = 1.0
    n_samples = int(fs * duration)
    t = np.arange(n_samples, dtype=np.float64) / fs

    # C-major triad fundamentals
    fundamentals = {
        "C4": 261.63,
        "E4": 329.63,
        "G4": 392.00,
    }

    # Include the fundamental plus 2nd and 3rd harmonic overtones
    harmonic_orders = (1, 2, 3)

    def log_decay_amplitude(order: int) -> float:
        """
        Logarithmic amplitude decay normalized so that the fundamental has
        amplitude 1:

            A(h) = log(2) / log(h + 1)

        A(1) = 1.000
        A(2) = 0.631
        A(3) = 0.500
        """
        return float(np.log(2.0) / np.log(order + 1.0))

    # Synthesize the mixed temporal signal
    x = np.zeros(n_samples, dtype=np.float64)
    expected = []

    for note, f0 in fundamentals.items():
        for h in harmonic_orders:
            f = h * f0
            a = log_decay_amplitude(h)
            x += a * np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * f * t)
            expected.append((f, f"{note} h{h}"))

    # Normalize to avoid clipping and make peak-detection thresholds stable
    time_peak = np.max(np.abs(x))
    if time_peak > 0:
        x /= time_peak

    # Hann window reduces spectral leakage for cleaner peak extraction.
    # For a raw unwindowed FFT, replace this with np.ones(n_samples).
    window = windows.hann(n_samples, sym=False)
    xw = x * window

    # Real-valued FFT
    X = rfft(xw)
    freqs = rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1.0 / fs)
    mag = np.abs(X)

    # Coherent-gain correction for the Hann window
    mag *= 2.0 / (n_samples * np.mean(window))
    mag[0] = 0.0

    max_mag = np.max(mag)
    if max_mag == 0:
        print("No signal detected.")
        return

    # Extract prominent spectral peaks
    peaks, _ = find_peaks(
        mag,
        height=0.05 * max_mag,
        prominence=0.02 * max_mag,
        distance=2,
    )

    df = fs / n_samples
    tol_hz = 2.0

    print("Detected FFT frequency peaks")
    print("Index\tFreq (Hz)\tMagnitude\tIdentified harmonic(s)")
    print("-" * 72)

    if peaks.size == 0:
        print("No prominent peaks detected.")
    else:
        for idx in peaks:
            # Quadratic interpolation gives a sub-bin frequency estimate
            if 0 < idx < len(mag) - 1:
                y0, y1, y2 = mag[idx - 1], mag[idx], mag[idx + 1]
                denom = y0 - 2.0 * y1 + y2
                delta = 0.0 if denom == 0 else 0.5 * (y0 - y2) / denom
                delta = float(np.clip(delta, -0.5, 0.5))
                peak_freq = freqs[idx] + delta * df
            else:
                peak_freq = freqs[idx]

            # Identify the peak by matching it to expected harmonic frequencies
            matches = [
                label
                for f, label in expected
                if abs(f - peak_freq) <= tol_hz
            ]
            label = " / ".join(matches) if matches else "unmatched"

            print(f"{idx}\t{peak_freq:8.2f}\t{mag[idx]:8.4f}\t{label}")

    # Print the theoretical harmonic frequencies for comparison
    print("\nExpected harmonic frequencies (Hz):")
    for f, label in sorted(expected):
        print(f"{label:10s} {f:8.2f}")

The discrete Fourier transform, or DFT, maps a finite sequence of \(N\) time-domain samples \(x[n]\) into \(N\) complex frequency-domain coefficients \(X[k]\) through the expression \(X[k] = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] e^{-j2\pi kn/N}\). Each coefficient is the inner product of the sampled signal with a complex exponential basis function whose discrete frequency is \(f_k = k f_s / N\), where \(f_s\) is the sampling rate. These basis functions are mutually orthogonal, so the DFT decomposes the waveform into a sum of sinusoidal components. For real-valued audio, the spectrum is conjugate symmetric, meaning that only the non-redundant half of the spectrum must be computed, as done here with a real FFT. The magnitude \(|X[k]|\) estimates spectral energy at each frequency bin, while the phase \(\arg(X[k])\) estimates temporal alignment. Because the DFT implicitly assumes periodicity, a finite recording whose tones do not contain an integer number of cycles leaks energy into neighboring bins; windowing, such as the Hann window used in the script, tapers the signal to reduce leakage at the cost of broadening each spectral peak.

In psychoacoustics, pitch is primarily associated with the fundamental frequency, whereas timbre is the perceptual quality that distinguishes instruments playing the same pitch at the same loudness. This distinction is largely governed by the harmonic spectrum: the relative amplitudes, phases, and temporal envelopes of partials at integer multiples of the fundamental. A logarithmically decaying overtone series, as synthesized here, approximates the common acoustic tendency for higher partials to carry less energy, producing a tone that is less bright than one with strong high harmonics. The C-major triad also illustrates spectral interaction: the second harmonic of G4 at 784.00 Hz and the third harmonic of C4 at 784.89 Hz nearly coincide, creating beating, roughness, or fusion depending on amplitude, phase, and auditory critical bandwidth. Thus, even when the fundamental pitches are identical, changing the overtone amplitudes changes the perceived instrument identity, which is why harmonic spectra are central to computational models of timbre.

The time-frequency uncertainty principle, also called the Gabor limit, states that a signal cannot be simultaneously localized with arbitrary precision in time and frequency. For a windowed analysis, the product of the effective time spread \(\Delta t\) and frequency spread \(\Delta f\) has a lower bound, commonly expressed as \(\Delta t \Delta f \geq 1/(4\pi)\) when spreads are defined as standard deviations. In discrete terms, a 1-second frame sampled at 44.1 kHz gives a nominal frequency resolution of \(f_s/N = 1\) Hz, so two components separated by less than about 1 Hz—such as 784.00 Hz and 784.89 Hz—cannot be resolved as distinct peaks by a single FFT. Shorter windows improve temporal localization of attacks and transients but broaden spectral peaks; longer windows sharpen frequency estimates but smear rapid changes. This constraint is mathematical rather than merely algorithmic, and it motivates fundamental trade-offs in spectrograms, filter banks, musical timbre analysis, and any DSP system that must represent both when and what frequencies are present.
